text:
some scattered thoughts on Isaacson's bio of Franklin + the man himself, virtues, vices, character studies, foils...the objective and unbiased presentation of "a man in full."

split into 10 sections / prob shouldve been an article

--

1. Munger's adulation of this man is not straightforward to me at all

munger was what led me in this direction, and I think from the angle of pragmatism, that "homespun American" outlook on life, and all those maxims (which only 1 out of 10 belong to Frankin himself), you can sort of connect the dots

but a lot of the other stuff will have you shaking your head. the way he went about shit, its hard to see how exactly Munger would approve...very manipulative, hypocritical, indirect, not adjectives you'd associate with Munger.

Isaacson on the use of pseudonyms -- "allowed [Franklin] to revel in gossip, and circumvent his personal pledge to speak ill of no one."

2. reputation vs reality

i'm not sure how many ppl have actually studied Franklin, the bio most people point to is the Van Doren one, from 1938, which is 850 pages...Isaacson's arguably supplants that

but Franklin kind of just gets bucketed in the "founding father" archetype, honest and direct, when in reality he's like the anti-founding father

the true founding father archetypes (like an Adams) had a strong antipathy towards him

some of what I write here may be off base but I also believe that you can't really speak on a man's character without reading at least one bio

and so I can't help but be skeptical on how many ppl's opinions on Franklin are truly well-informed

if ur well-informed, push back on anything here, but cite ur sources. I have no strong bias, just trying to call balls and strikes

3. impact on history

I don't want it to seem like I'm criticizing the man unnecessarily -- in terms of a single human's impact on history, Franklin is as substantial as you'll ever see.

not just the various inventions and discoveries and theories, but his involvement in every key American piece of legislature, plus his diplomacy with England and France all throughout the war

its all astounding in a positive way, any criticism of his character is to be viewed first thru that lens

I'd sum this all up as, his deeds are greater than ppl think, but his character is worse -- probably a wash or maybe even "upside to consensus"

I've bounced some of this off friends who are very well-read (albeit not on this particular man), response tends to be "guy must have a hell of a PR team," so ur not wrong if some of this catches u off guard

4. Franklin should probably be studied by anyone young and full of ideas

time and time again in the bio, you see things that are credited to him

but where you're like..."wait, THAT'S the reason we do things?" or "we didnt have this understood prior to 1750? wtf?"

pretty much.

a lot of history is no different than that meme:

"source?" 
"I made it up."

a person comes up with something, everyone else sort of looks at one another with a shrug like "shit, I guess that works," and then it becomes embedded in how mankind rolls

you see this over and over and cant help but laugh

so dont underestimate the impact that you as one individual could make on history, most of what we view as law was just the result of some dude with clout who threw a lot of shit at the wall.

5. the "come up"

its hard to read about franklin's come up and not have a bad taste in your mouth, very dirty, lots of foul play, sneaky, deceitful, Isaacson does a good job holding him accountable

its like Balzac's "behind every fortune is a crime"

Franklin was basically a propagandist or the original tabloid journalist before he was who he was

the freemasons turned him down, so he'd publish anonymous slander and lies until they relented. then, he'd publish positive stuff instead. stuff like that. Chesterfield's "coarse pulleys and dirty ropes," ad infinitum.

...all while holding himself out as a plain dealer.

that's what history tends to have an issue with. not who u are in public/private, so much as the width of the gap between those two. 

6. public vs private

history tends to be okay with immoral men who dont hold dont hold themselves out as moral.

what history loathes are 1. cowards and 2. hypocrites. Franklin falls squarely into the latter category throughout a lot of his life.

as a foil, you can be a Talleyrand (Duff Cooper's bio is solid) bc even though he was a snake, you knew who he was...he wasn't preaching virtue, he was always going to be on the winning team, and he was going to knife u in the back if it came down to it.

100 years from now Trump will prob be bucketed similarly -- somewhat of a rogue, but aligned public/private. no one denies the knavery, its whether u own it - he generally seems to.

but if ur preaching virtue in public, u better back that shit up in private. another foil is TR who preached to excess, but he backed it up so u cant really say shit.

anyone except TR would've gotten the label "sanctimonious cocksucker"

same with Chernow's Washington...not much gap between who he was in public vs private, vs how posterity views him
 
compare to Franklin who preached, while sometimes living what he preached, but most of the time not at all.

a final foil is Rousseau -- both Franklin's "autobiography" and Rousseau's "confessions" are alike in that they're a book about somebody...but history doesn't hold back, like, the guy in that book, he sure as fuck isn't you lol.

7. personality type

thru Isaacson's lens -- which is an unbiased one, and is the only one I'm referencing here -- Franklin was very much a social climber and user, loaded w/ snake-like behavior, and throughout his life you see how he ended up with no friends and horrible relationships start-to-finish.

especially with his wife, plus one of the worst endings to any father-son relationship I can remember reading about

some men have critics and enemies solely from being great...in Franklin's case, he had a ton but they were all well-deserved, and they were the type of men (mostly puritanical) who you don't really want as enemies, bc they walk the walk and they see that u arent.

I'm reading Master of the Senate now, on LBJ, he skews far more Franklin than Washington...has enemies for the same reason ("we see that u are a brown-nosing snake.")

so be careful blindly Franklin in the "honest founding father" bucket, that's not who he was, someone who reads is gonna side-eye that statement

and be cautious when you see someone put him in that bucket, bc it either shows something negative abt themselves, or it shows they dont do their homework -- neither are wonderful.

8. the adams/franklin foil

one of the most interesting foils is between adams and Franklin

adams is much closer to a Washington type, the upright founding father, puritan, moral, brutally honest

franklin was avuncular, loveable, a gifted diplomat, pragmatic, somewhat of a flaneur, often lazy, rising at noon and then spending all day lounging around with young women

but adams and Franklin were forced thru circumstance to spend time together and it shines light into each man's character

adams lacked Franklin's social graces, Franklin lacked Adams' integrity

a fantastic quote (the "easy gesture" one, bolded):

--

"Adams, who was 42 when he arrived, was thirty years younger than Franklin and about five years younger than Franklin’s son, William. More sensitive to insults, real and imagined, Adams came to feel more strongly about Franklin than vice versa. At times, he was driven almost to distraction by Franklin’s insouciance and self-indulgence. “He envied—and suspected—people with no rough edges, people who moved easily in the finer circles,” Berkeley historian Robert Middlekauff writes of Adams in his textured study Benjamin Franklin and His Enemies. He was “incapable of the easy gesture, and incapable too of the small hypocrisies that carry other men through life.” David McCullough, in his masterly biography of Adams, is more sympathetic and balanced about him, but he too conveys the rich complexity of his attitudes toward Franklin."

--

the "small hypocrisies that carry men through life" phrase still has me meditating...I hate hypocrisy and I suck at tact, but perhaps I need to rethink my priors.

anyway I think a lot of ink has been spilled on this relationship (adams/franklin) but its worth investigating in that prob tells you something about yourself

I felt adams' side more -- I would've prob snapped on this dude...like "u disloyal rat motherfucker" lol. 

I bucket guys like him as "avoid." you don't want them as a friend, nor do you want them as an enemy. just avoid.

I worship TR and I can't help but feel like TR, man-to-man, would have had problems with him. bc TR was thorough for real.

but as with any great man, franklin's vices and virtues were inseparable. his ability to be a bullshit artist is exactly what made him a great diplomat -- easily the greatest American diplomat of all time -- and create compromise where none would have existed.

that's what allowed him to singlehandedly shape the outcome of the American revolution.

so dont view this post as overly negative, nitpicky, critick-y, or a haterade bath...its all just a portrait of a man in full. and as is tradition, there is no line between a man's virtues and his vices. they tend to be two sides of the same coin.

9. overall bio review

I was almost halfway thru the bio and ready to give it a bad review

I think Isaacson lingers too long on parts of Franklin's early life that aren't all that impactful (all the weird relationships with young women that werent his wife, screwing people over, "war with poisoned arrows," etc)

but what you have to understand is that Franklin's life is extremely back-half weighted

all the other founding fathers were 20's and 30's, franklin was like 81 when this was all going down...he was born in 1706, you can do the math

so the bio itself is back-half weighted

by the end, the review went from "eh" to "excellent"

Isaacson does a fantastic job not only addressing the bios before his (Van Doren) and incorporating secondary material/feedback, but goes above and beyond in how Franklin was viewed over the years, the assaults on him by the Romantics, and so on

I've never been sure what to say on Isaacson as a biographer because the ones I've read have been on living people (Jobs, Musk) slash recently deceased, which doesn't really feel right...u gotta let the body get cold first, that Musk bio was interesting but there's too much football left to play

it'll take a few hundred years to see where some of his bios measure up

clearly all the awards and accolades cant be denied, I think he's labeled as the best of our generation, I'm not one to dispute that

and I've never known him as anything but even-keeled, not a biased biographer, straight facts...almost too bland at times.

but I think in this Franklin bio he really showed his skill, and he presents "A Man in Full" -- the good and the bad -- with a deft hand.

that's what all my opinions here are based on, so if ur offended (idk why you would be) don't attack me, take it up with Isaacson.

10. what makes a great bio?

fuck the hero worship, fuck the "consensus view," I'd ask grok if I wanted that...see for urself, then ask where they sourced their info. Franklin's autobio, DUH lol.

Isaacson wrote his in 2003 -- its copyrighted material, its not in the LLM knowledge base, nor should it be. 

Hence why u gotta read bios to know the truth.

that's what makes a great bio, to me at least -- give the reader all the good and all the bad and we'll dig through it for our own benefit.

Isaacson does that marvelously well here.

very curious to get feedback from others (esp those who agree bc this feels like a wildly out-of-consensus take).

overall grade A bio -- top 15, maybe top 10 bios I've read.
